heading|1|1|Towards zero pollution in Europe|1|1|art-editorial|5|4|kicker=Editorial;standfirst=Last spring, a coronavirus reshaped the world in a matter of weeks. Many of the things that we had taken for granted were suddenly not available to us anymore. The pandemic caught the world by surprise, but, if you had asked a scientist working in a field related to infectious diseases, this was only a matter of time.;style=art-editorial||:Towards zero pollution in Europe||||
heading|1|2|Improving air quality improves people’s health and productivity|1|1|art-aire|11|10|kicker=Air;standfirst=Europe’s air quality has improved significantly over recent decades but pollutants still harm our health and the environment. heading|1|3|Ensuring clean waters for people and nature|1|1|art-agua|17|16|kicker=Water;standfirst=Water covers more than 70 % of the Earth’s surface and is essential to all life on our planet. Of all the Earth’s water, 96.5 % is contained within the oceans as salt water, whereas the remaining 3.5 % is freshwater — lakes, rivers, groundwater and ice. Good management of this limited and precious resource is indispensable for the well-being of people and nature.;style=art-agua||:Ensuring clean waters for people and nature||||

heading|1|4|Land and soil pollution — widespread, harmful and growing|1|1|art-suelo|23|22|kicker=Land and soil;standfirst=What do many vineyards scattered across idyllic landscapes, industrial sites and landfills have in common? The presence of chemicals might be the answer. From heavy metals to organic pollutants and microplastics, the soil in which we grow our food and the land on which we build our homes might be contaminated with different pollutants. Contaminants are widespread and are accumulating in Europe’s land and soils. How can we tackle this problem?;style=art-suelo||:Land and soil pollution — widespread, harmful and growing||||

heading|1|5|Living healthily in a chemical world|1|1|art-quimicos|27|26|kicker=Chemicals;standfirst=We can categorise pollution by where we find it — in soil, water or air — or we can look at different pollution types, such as chemicals. Synthetic chemicals are all around us. Some of them, however, can also be very harmful to our health and the environment. How can we limit the negative effects of chemicals that have become a part of our current way of life? Professor Geert Van Calster;style=art-quimicos||:Living healthily in a chemical world||||

heading|1|6|Does the polluter pay?|1|1|art-quien-contamina-paga|35|34|kicker=Interview;standfirst=A simple but powerful idea lies at the heart of environmental laws in the EU: the ‘polluter pays’ principle. This principle has been applied in the form of taxes, fines and other measures, such as quotas for pollutant emissions and the Environmental Liability Directive. We talked to Professor Geert Van Calster about this principle, its benefits and shortcomings.;style=art-quien-contamina-paga||:Does the polluter pay?||||
heading|1|7|The challenge of reducing industrial pollution|1|1|art-industria|39|38|kicker=Industry;standfirst=Industrial pollution in Europe is decreasing, thanks to a blend of regulation, developments in manufacturing and environmental initiatives. heading|1|8|Noise pollution is still widespread across Europe, but there are ways to reduce the volume|1|1|art-ruido|45|44|kicker=Noise;standfirst=Many of us are increasingly confronted by noise in our daily lives. Loud cars on the street, a low-flying plane overhead or a nearby train often bring with them annoyance and frustration. However, their impact on our health and environment could be a lot worse than you think. Francesca Racioppi;style=art-ruido||:Noise pollution is still widespread across Europe, but there are ways to reduce the volume||||
